title: Preorder visit order
question: In a preorder traversal of a binary tree, in which order are the nodes of each subtree handled?
options: The left subtree first, then the node itself, and finally the right subtree
The node itself first, then its left subtree, and finally its right subtree
The left subtree first, then the right subtree, and finally the node itself
The node itself first, then its right subtree, and finally its left subtree
explanation: Preorder visits the node before descending into its children, going left before right. That is why it suits copying or serializing a tree, since a parent always appears before its descendants. Visiting the node between the subtrees is inorder, and visiting it last is postorder.

title: Data structure behind level-order
question: Which auxiliary data structure lets a level-order (breadth-first) traversal visit nodes one depth at a time?
options: A stack, so the most recently discovered child is always processed next
A priority queue ordered by node value, so smaller values are visited first
A hash set of visited nodes, which alone fixes the order in which nodes are taken
A queue, so nodes are processed in the same order in which they were discovered
explanation: A first-in, first-out queue guarantees that every node at depth d is dequeued before any node at depth d + 1. A stack would produce a depth-first order instead. A priority queue orders by value rather than depth, and a visited set only prevents repeats without defining any order.

title: Base case of a recursive traversal
question: A recursive function visits every node of a binary tree by calling itself on the left and right children. What is the usual base case that stops the recursion?
options: The current node is empty (null), so the function returns without doing anything
The current node has no children, so the function returns before touching it
The current node holds the smallest value seen so far, so the function stops there
The current node was already visited once, so the function returns to its caller
explanation: Every call that reaches an empty child must return immediately, otherwise the function would try to read the fields of a missing node. Stopping at a leaf is not enough, because a node with only one child would still call itself on the missing side. Tracking visited nodes or minimum values is unnecessary in a tree, which has no cycles.

title: Why postorder frees a tree
question: A program must release the memory of every node in a binary tree manually. Why is a postorder traversal the natural choice for this job?
options: It reaches the deepest nodes first, so a node is freed only after its children are gone
It visits the root first, so the whole tree becomes unreachable in a single step at the start
It uses less memory than other traversals because it never needs recursion or a stack
It visits nodes in sorted order, which lets the program free the smallest values before the larger ones
explanation: Postorder handles both subtrees before the node itself, so a parent is released only after its children have been. Visiting the root first would lose the pointers to the children before they could be freed. Postorder still needs recursion or an explicit stack, and sorted order only holds for inorder on a search tree.

title: Stack space of a recursive traversal
question: A recursive depth-first traversal visits a binary tree with n nodes and height h. How much call-stack space does it use at the deepest point?
options: Proportional to n, because every node of the tree has its own pending call at that point
Proportional to log n in every case, because each call halves the number of remaining nodes
Proportional to h, because only the calls along the current root-to-node path are pending
Constant, because each call finishes completely before the next child is explored at all
explanation: At any moment the pending calls form a single path from the root down to the node being visited, so the stack depth is at most the height h. For a balanced tree that is about log n, but for a degenerate chain it grows to n. Calls on a path do wait for their children, so the space is not constant, and nodes in other branches are not pending.

title: The three steps of divide and conquer
question: Which sequence correctly describes the structure of a divide-and-conquer algorithm?
options: Guess a solution, verify it on a small input, and then repeat the guess on a larger input
Build a table of every possible subproblem and then read the final answer from its last cell
Split the problem into smaller subproblems, solve each recursively, and combine their results
Pick the locally best choice at each step and never revisit any earlier decision that was made
explanation: Divide and conquer divides the input into smaller instances of the same problem, solves them recursively (with a base case for tiny inputs), and merges the partial answers. Filling a table of all subproblems describes dynamic programming, and always taking the locally best choice describes a greedy strategy. Guess-and-verify is not a general algorithm design paradigm.

title: Why binary search is logarithmic
question: Binary search on a sorted array of n items takes O(log n) time. What property of the algorithm explains this?
options: Each comparison checks two items at once, so the number of steps is cut to n divided by 2
Each comparison discards half of the remaining range, so only about log n halvings are possible
The array is copied into a balanced tree first, and walking that tree always costs log n
The algorithm sorts the array as it goes, and the sorting work is spread over all the steps
explanation: After each comparison with the middle element, one half of the range can be ruled out, and an input of size n can be halved only about log2 n times before one element remains. Checking two items per step would still leave a linear number of steps. Binary search needs no copy into a tree and does not sort anything, because the input must already be sorted.

title: The combine step of merge sort
question: In merge sort, the two halves of an array have already been sorted recursively. What does the combine step do?
options: It swaps elements around a chosen pivot so smaller values end up on its left side and larger values on its right
It inserts each element of the right half into a binary search tree built from the elements of the left half
It concatenates the two halves unchanged, since each half is sorted and the whole must be too
It repeatedly takes the smaller front element of the two sorted halves to build one sorted array
explanation: Merging walks both sorted halves with two indices and always copies the smaller front element, which takes linear time. Partitioning around a pivot belongs to quicksort, where the work happens before the recursive calls. Simply concatenating two sorted halves does not give a sorted array, because their value ranges may interleave.

title: Base case in divide and conquer
question: Why must a divide-and-conquer algorithm define a base case for very small inputs?
options: It stops the repeated splitting, since an input that cannot shrink further is solved directly
It lets the algorithm choose between recursion and loops depending on the machine's available memory
It guarantees that the subproblems are always solved in parallel on separate processor cores
It stores previously computed answers so that the same subproblem is never solved twice
explanation: Without a base case the recursion would keep dividing forever and eventually overflow the call stack. Small inputs such as an empty array or a single element are solved directly, and the larger answers are built from them. Caching answers is memoization, parallel execution is an optional optimisation, and neither replaces the need to stop the recursion.

title: Divide and conquer versus dynamic programming
question: What is the key difference between the subproblems of merge sort and those of a naive recursive Fibonacci function?
options: Merge sort works only on arrays, while Fibonacci recursion works only on integer inputs
Merge sort subproblems are independent and disjoint, while Fibonacci subproblems overlap heavily
Merge sort recursion is always iterative underneath, while Fibonacci recursion never terminates
Merge sort subproblems must be solved in sequence, while Fibonacci ones can run at the same time
explanation: The two halves of an array share no elements, so no subproblem is ever computed twice. Fibonacci calls such as fib(n - 1) and fib(n - 2) both need fib(n - 3), so the same values are recomputed many times and caching them pays off. The input types are not the real distinction, both recursions terminate, and independent subproblems are in fact the ones that parallelise easily.

title: What backtracking does
question: Which description best fits a backtracking algorithm?
options: It sorts all possible candidate solutions first and then picks the best one found in that list
It stores the answer to each subproblem in a table and combines those answers bottom-up
It repeatedly splits the input in half and solves each half independently of the other half
It builds a candidate solution step by step and undoes the latest choice when it leads nowhere
explanation: Backtracking explores a tree of partial solutions depth first, and when a partial solution cannot be completed it steps back and tries the next choice. Generating and sorting every candidate is plain brute force. Tables of subproblem answers belong to dynamic programming, and halving the input is divide and conquer.

title: Pruning in backtracking
question: In a backtracking search, what does pruning mean?
options: Removing duplicate entries from the final list of solutions after the search has completed
Skipping a whole branch of the search as soon as a partial solution is known to be invalid
Limiting the recursion to a fixed maximum depth chosen before the search is started
Running the search again from the beginning with a smaller input after a failure occurs
explanation: Pruning cuts off a subtree of candidates the moment a constraint is violated, so none of its descendants is ever generated. That is what makes backtracking faster than exhaustive enumeration. Deduplicating at the end still does all the work, a fixed depth cap may miss valid solutions, and restarting on a smaller input is not part of the technique.

title: Choose, explore, unchoose
question: A backtracking function appends a value to a path list, calls itself, and then removes the value again. Why is the removal needed?
options: The path list would otherwise grow past the memory limit of the recursion's call stack
The recursive call returns a copy of the path, so the original list must be emptied first
The next sibling choice must start from the same state the parent call had before this choice
The removal is what marks the current branch as invalid so the search will skip it later
explanation: The same list is shared by all calls, so a choice left in it would leak into the sibling branches and produce wrong paths. Undoing the choice restores the parent's state before the next option is tried. The list lives on the heap and not in stack frames, the recursive call does not hand back a copy, and marking a branch invalid is the job of the constraint check.

title: Size of the permutation search space
question: A backtracking algorithm generates every ordering of n distinct items with no pruning at all. How many complete orderings does it produce?
options: n factorial, because there are n choices for the first slot, then n - 1, and so on
n squared, because each item is compared with every other item exactly once
2 to the power n, because each item is either included or excluded in the ordering
n times log n, because the items are repeatedly split into two groups of equal size
explanation: The first position can hold any of n items, the second any of the remaining n - 1, and so on, giving n * (n - 1) * ... * 1 = n! orderings. The value 2 to the n counts subsets, where each item is only included or excluded. Neither n squared nor n log n grows nearly fast enough, which is why unpruned permutation search becomes impractical past roughly a dozen items.

title: A problem suited to backtracking
question: Which of these problems is a classic fit for backtracking?
options: Finding the maximum value in an unsorted array of integers in a single pass
Looking up the value for a key in a hash table that already holds the data
Placing eight queens on a chessboard so that no two of them attack each other
Reversing the characters of a string by swapping its first and last positions
explanation: Placing queens means making a sequence of choices under constraints, where a conflicting placement forces the search to step back and try another square. Sudoku and maze solving work the same way. The other tasks have a direct single-pass or constant-time solution and need no search through partial solutions.

title: Overlapping subproblems
question: What does it mean that a problem has overlapping subproblems?
options: The same smaller subproblems are needed again and again while solving the larger problem
The input can be split into two halves that share no elements and are solved separately
The best answer is always made by choosing the locally cheapest option at each step
Every subproblem has to be solved in parallel before the main problem can be started
explanation: Overlap means the recursion tree contains many identical subproblems, for example fib(3) appearing under both fib(4) and fib(5). That repetition is what makes caching or tabulating their answers worthwhile. Disjoint halves describe divide and conquer, and always picking the locally cheapest option describes a greedy strategy.

title: Optimal substructure
question: What does optimal substructure mean for a dynamic programming problem?
options: The whole problem always has exactly one valid solution that every algorithm will eventually find
The subproblems are arranged in a tree whose depth never grows beyond the logarithm of the input
An optimal solution can only be found by checking every combination of choices one after another
An optimal solution to the whole problem can be built from optimal solutions to its subproblems
explanation: Optimal substructure lets the recurrence combine the best answers of smaller states into the best answer of a larger one, as in the shortest path through an intermediate node. It does not say the solution is unique, bounds nothing about tree depth, and is in fact the property that lets dynamic programming avoid checking every combination.

title: Memoization versus tabulation
question: What is the difference between memoization and tabulation in dynamic programming?
options: Memoization works only on numbers, while tabulation works on strings and on arrays only, never on graphs
Memoization caches results of recursive calls on demand, while tabulation fills a table from small cases up
Memoization always uses less memory than tabulation, because it keeps only the final answer
Memoization finds approximate answers quickly, while tabulation is the only variant that is exact
explanation: Memoization is top-down: the recursive function runs as written and stores each result the first time it is computed. Tabulation is bottom-up: an iterative loop fills a table starting from the base cases. Both apply to any data type, both give exact answers, and memoization usually stores as many entries as the table does.

title: Naive versus memoized Fibonacci cost
question: A naive recursive `fib(n)` calls `fib(n - 1)` and `fib(n - 2)`. After adding a cache of computed values, how does the running time change?
options: It drops from linear time to constant time, because every value is already stored
It stays exponential, because the cache must still be searched on every recursive call
It drops from exponential time to linear time, because each value is computed only once
It drops from exponential time to logarithmic time, because the cache halves the problem
explanation: Without a cache the call tree roughly doubles at every level and takes exponential time. With a cache, fib(k) is computed once for each k from 0 to n and later calls are constant-time lookups, so the total is linear. A lookup costs constant time rather than undoing the gain, and the cache avoids repeats rather than halving the input.

title: Base cases in a DP table
question: When filling a dynamic programming table bottom-up, why must the base cases be initialised before the loop starts?
options: They set the size of the table, which must be known before any loop can be executed
They are the only cells whose values are checked when the algorithm returns its answer
They tell the loop how many times to run, so the number of iterations is fixed in advance
They hold the known answers of the smallest states, from which every other cell is derived
explanation: Each cell is computed from earlier cells through the recurrence, so some cells must already hold values that do not depend on anything else. Without them the first iterations would read uninitialised or wrong data and the error would propagate through the whole table. Table size and iteration count come from the problem's dimensions, and the final answer usually sits in a different cell.
